extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy and classics (readers of Plato)
extracted.subtask_description: Critical exposition of Books IX–X of Plato's Republic, especially Plato's account of pleasure, his numeric/figurative devices, and his sustained critique of poetry and the imitative arts. The page explains Plato's standards for judging pleasures, art, actors, and moral education (the myth of Er).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish kinds of pleasure (necessary / unnecessary / 'wild-beast')
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures should be classified: necessary and unnecessary pleasures (as earlier in the Republic and repeated by Aristotle), and a further class of 'wild beast' pleasures corresponding to base appetites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato accepts some pleasures (not all are bad as Cynics assert). He notes pleasures (e.g., smell, hope, anticipation) that have no antecedent pain. The classification helps judge which pleasures are proper to the several parts of the soul and which corrupt it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value pleasures of reason over sensual pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellectual pleasures are superior because they are 'at rest' and not fleeting; reason can judge lower pleasures while lower parts of the soul cannot judge pleasures of reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato contrasts the permanence and dignity of pleasures of knowledge with the relative, unreal, and transient character of sensual pleasures; the 'royal' pleasure (of reason) is pre-eminent since it can form judgments about lower pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid equating transience with unreality of pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume that because a pleasure is transient it is unreal; the ancients wrongly conflated transience of pleasure with unreality and the permanence of intellectual pleasure with the unchangeableness of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns that pleasures of knowledge, though more elevating, are not necessarily more lasting and depend on bodily conditions (cf. Introduction to Philebus). This temperates claims that intellectual pleasures are categorically more durable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of numerical/geometrical metaphors to express moral differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral and political differences may be expressed via arithmetic/geometrical images (e.g., Plato's interval of 729—the cube of 9—to mark the immeasurable gap between the kingly and tyrannical life).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato 'finds the natural vehicle of his thoughts in a progression of numbers' and sometimes forms numbers into geometric figures as rhetorical or speculative support. The passage cautions that abstract/formal expression can give a false sense of verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art/poetry is imitation and thrice removed from truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet (and painter) is an imitator whose work is at least three removes from the Form/truth (God makes the original, the craftsman makes the thing, the poet paints the thing — an imitation of an imitation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's famous bed-example: God (idea) → carpenter (maker) → painter (imitator). Because poets deal with appearances rather than realities, their creations cannot be taken as knowledge-bearing or authoritative about truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitators lack genuine knowledge and cannot be educators
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere imitation does not amount to science or true opinion; the imitator has no knowledge of the realities he depicts and so cannot supply instruction or authoritative guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text asserts: 'Imitation, then, is devoid of knowledge, being only a kind of play or sport,' and treats tragic and epic poets as 'imitators in the highest degree.' This underpins Plato's distrust of poetic authority over civic education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry injures by exciting the passions and enfeebling reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry and drama are dangerous because they stimulate and license emotions—pity, grief, buffoonery—that people would otherwise restrain, thereby weakening self-command and reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: long lamentations teach one to weep at one's own sorrows; comedy's coarse merriment can turn the spectator into a buffoon. For Plato these emotional appeals give the poet undue power over the inferior parts of the soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge poetry by its utility to the state and soul (not merely 'innocent pleasure')
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should be evaluated on whether it is useful—does it educate and make men better?—rather than on whether it merely gives innocent pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato asks 'What good have they done?' and proposes prohibition of poetry that goes beyond hymns/praises unless it can 'show that she is useful as well as delightful.' Supporters who are not poets may plead prose; poets must defend usefulness in verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible poetry: limited to hymns to gods and praise of famous men
rubrics_metrics.description: The Republic will 'prohibit all poetry which goes beyond hymns to the Gods and praises of famous men' unless poetry can demonstrate useful, soul-shaping effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Plato's practical restriction: only poetry that aligns with civic ideals and fosters virtue (e.g., religious hymns, encomia) is admissible; tragic/imitative poetry that enflames passions is to be excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting and dramatic talent may degrade character (actors as dangers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The profession of actor is seen as a degradation because 'one man in his life cannot play many parts'; repeated role-playing risks destroying the actor's own character, making him the slave of his art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato is 'more decided in his expulsion of the dramatic than of the epic poets' partly for this reason: dramatic or rhetorical power is often associated with weakness or dissolution of character, and thus can be politically and morally hazardous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider whether art ennobles or merely imitates appearances
rubrics_metrics.description: A central counter-criterion: judge whether art does more than copy appearances—whether it can ennoble humble subjects and express an ideal or 'divine' element beyond mere imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commentary notes that some art (Rembrandt, Turner, Pheidias) can endow ordinary objects with dignity or embody ideals that transcend Plato's simple imitation model. When art uplifts and harmonizes the soul it may be exculpated from Plato's criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should train choice: refuse evil and choose the good (myth of Er)
rubrics_metrics.description: Education must teach men the combinations of life and train them to choose lives that make the soul better — to 'refuse the evil and choose the good' with an 'iron sense of truth and right.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the myth of Er souls choose their next lives from varied samples; philosophical education equips one to choose wisely (avoid tyrannies, extremes) and thereby secure true happiness. The passage uses the selection-of-lives narrative to ground moral-educational aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral accounting: proportionate retribution and reward in the afterlife
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral order involves proportionate punishment/reward (e.g., for every evil deed souls are punished tenfold; rewards of virtue are likewise in proportion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The myth of Er supplies a standard of cosmic justice that reinforces why justice and the proper ordering of the soul are intrinsically advantageous: observable temporal goods pale compared with eternal or posthumous retribution/reward.
